cf.title: Batch fsyncs when recycling WAL segments

input.subject: [Patch] Batch fsyncs when recycling WAL segments

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived against 0001, which batches only unlinks and does not touch the WAL write path. For 0002, demand-1 and maintenance-fit-3 stand: every number measures background checkpoint cleanup time, and message #3 says it is "not a TPS result". 0002 adds a durability invariant to the WAL write path for that gain, and the author doubts in message #3 that it is worth the plumbing. Confidence is low because only the author has posted and the verdict rests on missing evidence.

brief.title: Batch fsyncs when removing and recycling WAL segments at checkpoint
brief.problem: A checkpoint that removes or recycles many WAL segments pays one pg_wal directory fsync per segment through durable_unlink() or durable_rename(). The author cites an earlier thread calling these fsyncs a real bottleneck. Systems with many segments per checkpoint, or small segment sizes, pay the most.
brief.proposed_design: 0001 unlinks all removable segments first, fsyncs pg_wal once, then removes their archive-status files; timeline-switch cleanup stays unbatched. 0002 (WIP) renames recycled segments in a batch, fsyncs the files and pg_wal once, and adds a timeline-qualified durability frontier in XLogCtl. XLogFileInit() fsyncs the segment and pg_wal itself when the frontier does not cover it or a recycle batch is active.
user_visible_surface: New injection point(s) in the WAL recycle path, used by TAP test 058_wal_recycle_durability.pl.
author_claims: Recycle batching cut checkpoint cleanup from a median of about 139 ms to 27 ms with about 44 segments recycled (ext4, Azure).
With 1 MiB segments and 512 MiB recycled, cleanup fell from 1900 ms to 80 ms.
0001 alone cut removal of 128 segments from 394 ms to 154 ms; one segment shows no change.
The write-path fallback should almost never fire because the checkpointer normally stays ahead.
0001 keeps the existing LOG-level policy on directory fsync failure and retains archive-status files so a later checkpoint retries.
brief.thread_state: Only the author has posted; four messages carry v1 to v4, with 0002 marked WIP and nocfbot. Three reviewers are listed in the CommitFest, but none has replied, and the author's question about a simpler invariant for 0002 is open.
unclear: No TPS or commit-latency numbers, so the effect on user workloads is unknown.
No benchmarks on filesystems other than ext4, or on storage with cheap fsync.
The thread does not say what cost the XLogFileInit() check adds on the hot WAL write path.
0002 leaves the active-batch marker set until restart after a failed batch, forcing the fallback on every new segment; the thread does not discuss this cost.
The thread does not say whether the frontier interacts safely with standbys, archive recovery or wal_init_zero.

prior_attempts.title: Speed up WAL file removal during recovery
prior_attempts.who_objected: Kyotaro HORIGUCHI, Michael Paquier, Fujii Masao
prior_attempts.quote: In short, if a crash happens in the code paths calling RemoveXlogFile with durable = false before fsync'ing pg_wal, then a rename has no guarantee to be durable, so you could finish again with a file that as an old name, but new contents.
prior_attempts.reason: Reviewers found that skipping the per-file fsync breaks crash safety for recycled segments: after a crash a renamed file can keep its old name but hold new contents, which brings back problems fixed by 1d4a0ab1. Deleting all files to avoid renames loses WAL recycling and costs performance. The alternatives (moving the work to the checkpointer, or disabling fsync in the durable_* functions around the loop) also drew objections. With no agreed design, Michael Paquier returned the entry with feedback.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P9 dropped per-file fsyncs in timeline-switch cleanup, where renames were mixed in, with no guard. 0001 batches only unlinks and leaves timeline-switch cleanup unbatched; 0002 batches renames but adds a write-path fallback fsync.

objections.title: Gain is shown only as background checkpoint cleanup time
objections.failure_scenario: A committer merges the recycle batching on the strength of a 139 ms to 27 ms cleanup saving. The checkpointer does this work in the background, so most users see no change in TPS or commit latency. The project keeps the added code with no measured user benefit.
objections.argument: Every number in messages #1, #2 and #3 measures checkpoint cleanup time. Message #3 says it is "not a TPS result". The only demand in the material is a second-hand note in message #1 that an earlier thread called these fsyncs a bottleneck. No field report, no -general or -bugs case, and no user stall caused by this cleanup appears.
objections.author_must_show: Which workload shows a user-visible stall, such as commit latency, WAL segment shortage or recovery time, caused by per-segment pg_wal fsyncs, and how large is it?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 cites an earlier thread that called these fsyncs a bottleneck, but that thread's content is not in the material. No message shows a user-visible effect, and message #3 says the numbers are not a TPS result.

objections.title: Write-path complexity paid by everyone for checkpointer-only time savings
objections.failure_scenario: A user on default settings upgrades and sees no TPS or latency change, because recycling already runs in the background. The project still carries the frontier logic on the WAL write path and must keep it correct in every later WAL change.
objections.argument: All numbers measure checkpoint cleanup time, and message #3 says "This is not a TPS result". The large gains appear with 1 MiB segments or 128 removed segments, which are unusual setups. 0001 gets part of the benefit without touching the write path. 0002's extra cost lands on shared code that all users run.
objections.author_must_show: Which workload shows lower commit latency or higher throughput from 0002 beyond what 0001 already gives?

critic.reasoning: The 44-segment case uses 16 MiB segments and ordinary settings, so the gain is not limited to unusual setups. Still, every number is cleanup time, and the author in message #3 doubts that 0002's plumbing is worth it.

other_surviving.title: Recycle durability frontier not shown to cover standby and recovery paths
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A standby's restartpoint batch-renames old segments. The walreceiver, or a segment restored from the archive, then lands in one of those names before the pg_wal fsync. The standby crashes, comes back with an old file name holding new contents, and the operator finds out when replay stops on a bad record or after promotion.
other_surviving.argument: 0002 keeps a renamed segment safe only if every writer passes the XLogFileInit() frontier check. The material shows this for the primary's WAL write path only. It does not cover restartpoints, walreceiver writes, archive restore or promotion, beyond saying the frontier is timeline-qualified. [P9] was returned because deferring the pg_wal fsync after a rename can leave a file with an old name and new contents. The author's own finding of a frontier hole in message #3 suggests other paths need the same proof.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which processes can create or write a WAL segment during a restartpoint or archive recovery, and how does each one reach the frontier check?

precedents.title: Speed up WAL file removal during recovery

critic.reasoning: The walreceiver opens new segments through XLogFileInit(), so that part of the scenario is weaker than stated. But the thread shows the frontier only for the primary's write path, and says nothing about restartpoints, archive restore or promotion.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: After a failed batch fsync, later fsyncs are trusted to finish the renames
other_surviving.failure_scenario: The batch fsync of pg_wal fails, and the kernel drops the dirty directory state. A backend's fallback fsync of pg_wal then reports success, and a commit goes into a recycled segment. A crash loses the rename, and the committed WAL is gone at the next startup.
other_surviving.argument: In 0002, a failed batch leaves the active-batch marker set until restart, and the server keeps running on per-segment fallback fsyncs. Postgres treats data file fsync failure as PANIC because a retried fsync can succeed after the data was lost. The proposal does not say why a retry is safe for the pg_wal entries of renames that will hold commit records. It also does not give the cost of taking the fallback on every new segment until restart.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why is a later successful fsync of pg_wal enough to make renames durable after the batch fsync failed, and why should 0002 not PANIC in that case?

critic.reasoning: Master also reports a failed recycle rename fsync at LOG level, which lowers the weight of this objection. But 0002 states that the server keeps running on fallback fsyncs after a failed batch, and does not say why a retried pg_wal fsync is trustworthy.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: 0002 spreads one durability invariant across checkpoint cleanup and WAL writes
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how segments are installed, for example in pre-allocation, walreceiver or wal_init_zero paths, without updating the frontier or the batch marker. A commit lands in a renamed segment whose directory entry is not durable. After a power loss the commit is gone, and only a test that forces an injection-point interleaving would notice.
other_surviving.argument: 0002 adds shared state in XLogCtl that every segment installer and XLogFileInit() must respect. v2 already had a hole in it, found by the author (message #3), and the author still asks whether a simpler invariant exists (messages #1, #3). [P9] stalled on the same crash hazard for renamed segments, where a crash after rename and before the directory fsync leaves an old name with new contents. No reviewer or committer has checked the new invariant yet.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Can the safety rule for recycled segments be kept inside one function, so that a future segment installer cannot bypass it without failing a test?

precedents.title: Speed up WAL file removal during recovery

critic.reasoning: Message #3 reports a hole in the v2 invariant, and the author still asks for a simpler one, so the concern stands. A redesign of 0002 could answer it and 0001 does not depend on it, so it is fixable.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Failed recycle batch moves directory fsyncs onto the WAL write path until restart
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A single transient error from the pg_wal directory fsync leaves the active-batch marker set. From then on, every segment switch by a backend or the WAL writer fsyncs the segment and pg_wal in the foreground, so commit latency rises with no error above LOG level, and it lasts until someone restarts the server.
other_surviving.argument: The 0002 commit message says "A failed batch leaves the marker set until restart." On master, this cost falls on the checkpointer. Under 0002, after one failure it falls on every session that crosses a segment boundary. The thread gives no number for the normal-case check in XLogFileInit() and none for this degraded mode.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What is the commit latency after a failed batch, and why should the marker not be cleared by the next successful batch?

critic.reasoning: The 0002 commit message states that a failed batch leaves the marker set until restart. The thread gives neither a cost for that mode nor a reason why a later successful batch cannot clear the marker.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Batched recycle renames reopen the crash hazard that stopped an earlier attempt
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch adds or changes a path that installs or opens a recycled segment without checking the durability frontier and the active-batch marker. A backend writes commit records into a segment whose rename is not yet durable, and the OS crashes. On restart the file has its old name and new contents, and no test or assertion caught it.
refuted.argument: [P9] was returned because deferring the pg_wal fsync lets a renamed file come back with its old name and new contents after a crash. 0002 brings back that window on purpose and closes it with a new invariant that spans the checkpointer and XLogFileInit(). The author found one hole in that invariant in v2 (message #3) and still asks for a simpler one (messages #1, #3). No reviewer has confirmed the invariant, and the proposal does not say what makes a future writer that bypasses it fail loudly.
refuted.author_must_show: Which invariant guarantees that every path writing WAL into a recycled segment, now and in future patches, sees a durable rename, and what fails if a path skips it?

precedents.title: Speed up WAL file removal during recovery

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which states the same bypass risk and asks a more concrete question. [P9] deferred the fsync with no guard, so it supports the hazard but not a judgment on the frontier design.

refuted.title: 0002 puts write-path cost on everyone for a narrow group
refuted.failure_scenario: Every backend that opens a new segment in XLogFileInit() now checks the frontier and the active-batch marker. After a failed batch the marker stays set until restart, so every new segment pays a file and pg_wal fsync. The users who gain are those recycling many segments per checkpoint or running with small segment sizes.
refuted.argument: The large gains in message #2 come from 1 MiB segments. With 64 MiB segments the saving is 25 ms per checkpoint. Message #3 calls 0002 "a fair amount of plumbing ... just to save these fsyncs". The thread gives no number for the write-path check or for the fallback after a failed batch. A committer would likely ask for 0001 alone until 0002's gain is shown to matter to more users.
refuted.author_must_show: How many installations recycle enough segments per checkpoint for 0002 to matter, and what does the XLogFileInit() check cost when nothing is recycled?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-3 for the question of who pays and who gains, and of maintenance-fit-2 for the cost after a failed batch. A shared-memory check once per new segment is also not a measurable cost for other users.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: Both patches change when pg_wal directory entries for removed and renamed segments become durable.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: 0002 changes how recycled WAL segments are installed and adds a timeline-qualified frontier in XLogCtl.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: 0002 adds shared state that the checkpointer, every segment installer and XLogFileInit() must keep consistent.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: 0002 adds a frontier and batch-marker check, and a possible file and pg_wal fsync, to XLogFileInit().

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: Gain is shown only as background checkpoint cleanup time

questions: Which workload shows a user-visible effect, such as commit latency, throughput or recovery time, from per-segment pg_wal fsyncs, and how large is it?
What does 0002 add in commit latency or throughput beyond what 0001 alone gives on the same workload?
Can the safety rule for recycled segments live in one function, so that a future segment installer cannot bypass it without failing a test?
Which processes can create or write a WAL segment during a restartpoint, archive recovery or promotion, and how does each one reach the frontier check?
After a failed batch fsync, why is a later pg_wal fsync trusted, and why does the marker stay set until restart?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows WAL segment installation and crash durability in xlog.c. Message #1 cc's two people from the earlier thread, but nobody other than the author has replied.
committability.liability: For 0002, the owner signs for crash safety of commits written into recycled segments, on primaries and standbys, for as long as the frontier exists. For 0001, the owner signs only for obsolete files that may reappear after a crash.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted four versions in three months, rebased twice, and reported and fixed a hole in the v2 invariant in message #3.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: This applies to 0002 only. A benchmark or field report where per-segment pg_wal fsyncs cause a measurable commit-latency, throughput or recovery-time problem, and where 0002 removes it beyond what 0001 does, would change the answer.

priority.reason: 0001 is small, limited to unlinks, and drew no objection, so it can go ahead by itself. 0002 is marked WIP, puts a new invariant on the WAL write path, and the author asks in messages #1 and #3 for a simpler one, while no user-visible gain is shown.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody checked whether the frontier and the active-batch marker cover every segment installer, or whether 0001's retry through the kept archive-status files works when archiving is off. Four level 2 objections against 0002 survived but were not evaluated here.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Deletion of the recycled future WAL files to free-up disk space if max_wal_size is reduced or wal_recycle is set to off
precedents_retrieved.summary: When max_wal_size is reduced or wal_recycle is set to off, a checkpoint should delete recycled future WAL files to free disk space. The author suggested keeping recycled WAL files in a sorted list and, at checkpoint, deleting them from the newest end, rebuilding the list after restart if needed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No patch was ever posted, so the commitfest entry had nothing to review. Jacob Champion closed it for that reason and invited the author to reopen it if a patch existed. Justin Pryzby supported the idea, and Tom Lane questioned only whether the behaviour was real.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
(This is registered in CF, but there doesn't seem to be a patch as part
of this thread, so I don't think there's anything to review.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes with durable_rename_excl()
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes with durable_rename_excl()
Reverted commit(s): Remove durable_rename_excl(); Replace existing durable_rename_excl() calls with durable_rename()
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commits 2c902bb and ccfbd92.  Per buildfarm members
kestrel, rorqual and calliphoridae, the assertions checking that a TLI
history file should not exist when created by a WAL receiver have been
failing, and switching to durable_rename() over durable_rename_excl()
would cause the newest TLI history file to overwrite the existing one.
We need to think harder about such cases, so revert the new logic for
now.

Note that all the failures have been reported in the test
025_stuck_on_old_timeline.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
Reverted commit(s): Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server Previously, we skipped a checkpoint if no WAL had been written since last checkpoint, though this does not appear in user documentation. As of now, we skip a checkpoint until we have written at least one enough WAL to switch the next WAL file. This greatly reduces the level of activity and number of WAL messages generated by a very low activity server. This is safe because the purpose of a checkpoint is to act as a starting place for a recovery, in case of crash. This patch maintains minimal WAL volume for replay in case of crash, thus maintaining very low crash recovery time.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 18fb9d8d21a28caddb72c7ffbdd7b96d52ff9724.  Per
discussion, it does not seem like a good idea to allow committed changes to
go un-checkpointed indefinitely, as could happen in a low-traffic server;
that makes us entirely reliant on the WAL stream with no redundancy that
might aid data recovery in case of disk failure.

This re-introduces the original problem of hot-standby setups generating a
small continuing stream of WAL traffic even when idle, but there are other
ways to address that without compromising crash recovery, so we'll revisit
that issue in a future release cycle.

precedents_retrieved.title: Unlogged relation copy is not fsync'd
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes the condition in RelationCopyStorage() so that the main and other non-init forks of an unlogged relation are fsync'd after copying, for example during alter table ... set tablespace. Without the fix, a checkpoint during the copy followed by a clean shutdown and power loss can lose part of the copied file.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author found that the posted patch was still incomplete and proposed a broader backpatchable fix that calls smgrimmedsync() for all but temporary relations, with similar changes in nbtsort.c, gistbuild.c and rewriteheap.c. Noah Misch questioned part of that analysis, and no revised patch followed. After about three months with no new version, Robert Haas marked the entry Returned with feedback as waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So it seems this has been waiting for
Heikki or someone else to have time to work it for the last 3 months.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_receivewal fail to streams when the partial file to write is not fully initialized present in the wal receiver directory
precedents_retrieved.summary: pg_receivewal fails to start when a leftover .partial segment is not fully zero-padded, for example after ENOSPC or a VM crash, so the user must delete the file by hand. The patch writes and pads a new segment under a temporary name, then renames it to the .partial name, and removes any leftover temporary file on the next call.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry stalled. After v9 in October 2022 no reviewer responded for more than 15 months, so Peter Smith returned it with feedback, citing low interest. Earlier, Michael Paquier said the fix does nothing for gzip or lz4 segments and that the real need is to reserve disk space for a full segment. He also asked why a temporary file is needed when the .partial file already serves that role. The visible messages do not show whether v9 answered these points.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since there seems not much interest, I have changed the status to "Returned with Feedback" [1].

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix calculations on WAL recycling
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes WAL recycling after commit 4b0d28de06 so that segments are removed and recycled based on the last checkpoint's redo pointer, not the prior one, which made min_wal_size not work as documented. It also changed recycling at timeline switch to use the switch point instead of a fixed 10 segments.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author removed the commitfest entry after Michael Paquier pointed out that the bug was already an open item for v11, so the fix would go through the open-items list. Paquier also objected to the timeline-switch change: a recycle point at the switch point can recycle segments still needed for crash recovery after promotion. The author dropped that part and posted a revised patch in the same thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This is an open item for v11.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fsync queue forgets requests on failure
precedents_retrieved.summary: Fix the checkpointer so that when an fsync of a relation segment fails during a checkpoint, the pending fsync request is kept for the next checkpoint instead of being dropped. The patch stops the pending-ops bitmapset from being lost when it is unlinked from the hashtable entry, merges unprocessed requests back on failure, and removes segments that succeeded as it goes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it as redundant with work in another thread (by Craig and Andres) that turns fsync I/O errors into PANICs and overhauls the request queue, because retrying fsync after a failure is useless on Linux. He noted that the other patch still left the retry path for errnos other than EIO and ENOSPC, but rejected this entry on the grounds that the issue would be resolved in that other thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Rejected, since this will have to be dealt with one way or another in
that other thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: speed up pg_rewind by using copy_file_range() and skipping some fsync
precedents_retrieved.summary: Two pg_rewind patches: one syncs only the files pg_rewind changed instead of the whole target data directory, and one uses copy_file_range() in place of read()+write() for local rewinds. The second adds a configure check and HAVE_COPY_FILE_RANGE and falls back to read()+write() on EXDEV or ENOTSUP.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier asked for pg_rewind benchmarks: many small files for the fsync patch, and large and small file sets on XFS with reflink for copy_file_range(). He also asked to drop the copy_file_range_support flag, because one EXDEV failure would turn copy_file_range() off for all other tablespaces and mount points, and to fix double-counted progress on fallback. The fsync patch skips files such as configuration files included from postgresql.conf. The visible messages do not show a reply after his last review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Anyway, I think that it would be good to do more benchmarking for this
patch first, and the patch you are proposing is enough for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Speed up WAL file removal during recovery
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Kyotaro HORIGUCHI, Michael Paquier, Fujii Masao
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch made RemoveNonParentXlogFiles() unlink old-timeline WAL files without a directory fsync after each one, and then fsync pg_wal once at the end. The aim was to cut about 2 seconds from failover at end of recovery when about 1,000 files are removed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers found that skipping the per-file fsync breaks crash safety for recycled segments: after a crash a renamed file can keep its old name but hold new contents, which brings back problems fixed by 1d4a0ab1. Deleting all files to avoid renames loses WAL recycling and costs performance. The alternatives (moving the work to the checkpointer, or disabling fsync in the durable_* functions around the loop) also drew objections. With no agreed design, Michael Paquier returned the entry with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
In short, if a crash happens in the code paths
calling RemoveXlogFile with durable = false before fsync'ing pg_wal,
then a rename has no guarantee to be durable, so you could finish again
with a file that as an old name, but new contents.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_receivewal fail to streams when the partial file to write is not fully initialized present in the wal receiver directory
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make the zero-padding of a new WAL segment in pg_receivewal atomic by padding a XXXX.partial.tmp file and then renaming it to XXXX.partial, durably when sync is on. A crash or ENOSPC during padding would then not leave a short .partial file that blocks restart until someone removes it by hand.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier said the temporary file only covers uncompressed segments, so gzip and lz4 segments can still fail midway, and that the real need is to reserve enough disk space before starting a segment. He also asked why a temporary file is needed when the .partial file already serves that role. Kyotaro Horiguchi preferred to error out with a hint to remove the bad file. The thread stops with these points open, and the visible messages do not show why the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: So the important part is not the pre-padding, it is to make sure that there is enough space reserved for the handling of a full segment before beginning the work on it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add more TAP coverage for archive status with crash recovery of standbys
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Add more TAP coverage for archive status with crash recovery of standbys
Reverted commit(s): Remove some unstable parts from new TAP test for archive status check
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This part of the test was included originally in 4e87c48, but got
reverted as of f9c1b8d because of timing issues in the test, where,
after more analysis, we found that the standbys may not have recovered
from the archives all the segments needed by the test.  This stabilizes
the test by making sure that standbys replay up to the position returned
by pg_switch_wal(), meaning that all segments are recovered before the
manual checkpoint that tests WAL segment recycling and its interactions
with archive status files.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert exporting of internal GUC variable "data_directory".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert exporting of internal GUC variable "data_directory".
Reverted commit(s): Use GUC lexer for recovery.conf parsing.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This undoes a poorly-thought-out choice in commit 970a18687f9b3058, namely
to export guc.c's internal variable data_directory.  The authoritative
variable so far as C code is concerned is DataDir; there is no reason for
anything except specific bits of GUC code to look at the GUC variable.

After yesterday's commits fixing the fsync-on-restart patch, the only
remaining misuse of data_directory was in AlterSystemSetConfigFile(),
which would be much better off just using a relative path anyhow: it's
less code and it doesn't break if the DBA moves the data directory of a
running system, which is a case we've taken some pains over in the past.

This is mostly cosmetic, so no need for a back-patch (and I'd be hesitant
to remove a global variable in stable branches anyway).

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert pg_wal_replay_wait() stored procedure
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert pg_wal_replay_wait() stored procedure
Reverted commit(s): Implement pg_wal_replay_wait() stored procedure; pg_wal_replay_wait(): Fix typo in the doc; Adjust pg_wal_replay_wait() procedure behavior on promoted standby; Improve header comment for WaitLSNSetLatches(); Add tests for pg_wal_replay_wait() errors
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 3c5db1d6b0, and subsequent improvements and fixes
including 8036d73ae3, 867d396ccd, 3ac3ec580c, 0868d7ae70, 85b98b8d5a,
2520226c95, 014f9f34d2, e658038772, e1555645d7, 5035172e4a, 6cfebfe88b,

precedents_retrieved.summary:
Apply a better fix to mdunlinkfork().
Reverted commit(s): Use TRUNCATE to preserve relfilenode for pg_largeobject + index.; Fix failure to remove non-first segments of temporary tables.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Replace the stopgap fix I made in 0e758ae89 with a cleaner one.

The real problem with 4ab5dae94 is that it contorted this function's
logic substantially, by introducing a third code path that required
different behavior in the function's main loop.  That seems quite
unnecessary on closer inspection: the new IsBinaryUpgrade case can
just share the behavior of the other immediate-unlink cases.  Hence,
revert 4ab5dae94 and most of 0e758ae89 (keeping the latter's
save/restore errno fix), and add IsBinaryUpgrade to the set of
conditions tested to choose immediate unlink.

Also fix some additional places with sloppy handling of errno,
to ensure we have an invariant that we always continue processing
after any non-ENOENT failure of do_truncate.  I doubt that that's
fixing any bug of field importance, so I don't feel it necessary to
back-patch; but we might as well get it right while we're here.

Also improve the comments, which had drifted a bit from what the
code actually does, and neglected to mention some important
considerations.

Back-patch to v15, not because this is fixing any bug but because
it doesn't seem like a good idea for v15's mdunlinkfork logic to be
significantly different from both v14 and v16.

roaster_notes.note: No prior-attempt objection against 0001: it batches only unlinks, and a lost unlink only leaves an obsolete file that a later checkpoint removes. The pre-allocating WAL files thread (message #1, [P15]) is where the idea came from; its withdrawal reason is not recorded.

The proposal changes no user-facing contract: no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object, pg_dump output, psql behaviour or client-visible change; the only new surface is a test injection point. Existing queries, scripts and dumps behave the same after upgrade. The one visible difference, obsolete WAL files reappearing in pg_wal after a crash in 0001, is removed by a later checkpoint and does not belong to this angle.
0001 deletes only segments already past the checkpoint and archiving, so files that come back after a crash look harmless, and I have no objection to it from this angle. The objections cover 0002.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It changes when the checkpointer fsyncs pg_wal while removing and recycling WAL segments, adds no SQL surface, GUC, role, view or setting, and gives unprivileged users no new action, data or timing signal; the only additions are internal injection points and a TAP test. Crash durability concerns belong to other angles.
0001 is small, separable and keeps the existing LOG-level policy. I have no maintenance objection to it alone.

No existing feature, option or extension does this job. A larger --wal-segsize (initdb or pg_resetwal) cuts the number of segments, and the author's numbers show the cost dropping with it, but it is a cluster-wide layout change and does not remove the per-segment fsyncs. The patch changes internal checkpointer behaviour that no extension or hook can reach, so the question of why it belongs in core does not apply.
0001 is small, adds no write-path cost, and has measured gains when many segments are removed. No demand objection is raised against 0001 on its own.
